title: Google Workspace (Docs, Sheets, Slides, Forms)
tagline: Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Forms and safe teamwork, with practice in every module
summary: Learn the tools millions of schools and teams use every day: organise and share files in Drive, write structured Docs, track and chart data in Sheets, build and present Slides, collect answers with Forms, and work together safely. Every module has practice labs that check your work and explain what is missing.

modules.title: Your account, Drive and sharing
modules.summary: Understand what a Google Account and Workspace are, keep files organised in Drive, and share them with exactly the right access.
modules.outcome: You can find your way around Drive, name and organise files, and share work safely with a person, a team or the world.
modules.intro: Google Workspace is a set of connected tools (Docs, Sheets, Slides, Forms, Drive, Gmail, Calendar and Meet) that live in the browser. Everything you make is saved automatically to the cloud, so you can open it on any device and work on it with other people at the same time. That changes how you work: you stop emailing copies and start sharing one living file.

topics.title: What Workspace is, and the account behind it
topics.html:
Everything starts with a Google Account. Your account holds your email address, your files in Drive, your calendar and your settings. A Workspace account is the version a school, company or club gets from an administrator; it works like a personal account, with extra controls set by the organisation (for example, who you may share files with).

The tools and what each is for
ToolUse it toLike
DriveStore, organise and share filesA cloud filing cabinet
DocsWrite text documentsA word processor
SheetsCalculate, track and chart dataA spreadsheet
SlidesBuild presentationsA presentation tool
FormsCollect answers with surveys and quizzesA survey builder
Gmail, Calendar, MeetEmail, schedule and video callMail, diary and meetings

What makes it different from desktop software

  • Autosave. There is no Save button; every change is saved as you type.
  • Real-time collaboration. Several people can edit one file at once and see each other's cursors.
  • Version history. Every change is recorded and you can go back.
  • Works anywhere. A browser and your account are all you need.
Tip

Look for the small cloud icon near the file name. A tick means everything is saved; a spinning icon means it is still saving, so do not close the tab yet.

Watch out

Your files belong to your account. If you use a school or work account, the organisation may be able to see and manage those files, and you may lose access when you leave. Keep personal files in a personal account.

Try it yourself: You are halfway through writing in Docs and your battery dies. Is your work lost?

Model answer. No. Docs saves automatically as you type, so open the file again on any device and your work is there, up to the last few seconds.

Check what you just learned

1. Which tool is mainly for collecting survey answers?
  • Docs
  • Forms (correct)
  • Sheets
  • Slides

Forms builds surveys and quizzes and gathers the answers.

2. What does autosave mean?
  • You must press Save often
  • Files are deleted after a week
  • Changes are saved as you type (correct)
  • Only the owner can save

Workspace tools save your changes continuously.
keyPoints: A Google Account holds your files, email and settings.
Workspace tools are linked and live in the browser.
Everything autosaves, and several people can edit at once.

topics.title: Drive: find, organise and name your files
topics.html:
Drive is where every file lives. The left-hand menu is your map; learn the main places and you will never lose a file.

Where things are in Drive
PlaceWhat is there
My DriveFiles and folders you own
Shared with meFiles other people gave you access to
RecentWhat you opened lately, a quick way back to work
StarredFiles you marked so they are easy to find
TrashDeleted files, kept for 30 days before they are removed for good
Shared drivesTeam-owned spaces in Workspace, where files stay when a person leaves
Worked example

A tidy structure for a school year

You have notes, assignments and group projects for four subjects.

  1. Make one folder for the year: 2026 School.
  2. Inside it make a folder per subject: Maths, Science, English, Computing.
  3. Inside each subject, make Notes, Assignments and Group work.
  4. Name files with the date first: 2026-03-14 Science Lab Report v2.

Answer. A file you can find in two clicks is a file you will use.

Naming rules that save time

  • Start with the date (year-month-day) so files sort in order.
  • Say what it is, not Untitled or Final.
  • Use v1, v2, v3 for versions; do not call anything Final.
  • Keep names short; avoid special characters.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving files as Untitled document.
  • Making folders inside folders ten levels deep.
  • Keeping everything on the Drive home screen.
  • Emptying the Trash without checking what is in it.
Tip

Press Shift+Z on a selected file to add it to a second folder without copying it, a shortcut: one file, two places.

Check what you just learned

1. Where do you find files other people shared with you?
  • Trash
  • Settings
  • Starred
  • Shared with me (correct)

Shared with me lists files others gave you access to.

2. Which file name is best?
  • 2026-03-14 Science Lab Report v2 (correct)
  • Final
  • Untitled document
  • asdf

It has a date, a clear subject and a version.
keyPoints: My Drive is yours; Shared with me is other people's files you can access.
Trash keeps deleted files for 30 days.
A date first, a clear name and a simple folder tree keep Drive usable.

topics.title: Sharing: the right access for each person
topics.html:
Click Share on any file and you decide who can open it and what they can do. Choosing carefully is the most valuable security skill in Workspace.

Access levels
RoleCanCannotGood for
ViewerRead, download (unless the owner turns it off)Change or commentParents, the public, final copies
CommenterRead, comment, suggest changesChange the text directlyTeachers and reviewers
EditorRead, change, and add people (unless restricted)Delete the file for the ownerCo-authors and partners
Who can open it
SettingMeaning
RestrictedOnly the people you add by name can open it
Anyone in your organisation with the linkEveryone in your school or company who has the link
Anyone with the linkAnyone in the world who has the link, with the role you choose
Worked example

Choose by purpose

You are sharing three things this week.

  1. The class newsletter for parents: Anyone with the link, Viewer. They read; nobody edits.
  2. Your essay draft for the teacher: the teacher by name, Commenter. They suggest; you decide.
  3. The group report with three classmates: each by name, Editor.

Answer. Start with the smallest access that gets the job done; you can always give more later.

Watch out

Anyone with the link, Editor means anyone who gets the link, even by accident, can change or delete your work. Use it almost never.

Habits that keep files safe

  • Add people by email address rather than sharing a public link when you can.
  • Look at the sharing list (the Share dialog) before you send a link.
  • When a project ends, remove people who no longer need access.
  • Share a folder for a project so new files inherit the same people.

Check what you just learned

1. A teacher should leave feedback without changing your words. Which role?
  • Viewer
  • Commenter (correct)
  • Editor
  • Owner

Commenters can comment and suggest but not rewrite.

2. What does 'Anyone with the link' mean?
  • Only people you named
  • Only your school
  • Anyone in the world who has the link (correct)
  • Nobody

Anyone who has the link can open it with the role you chose.

Key terms: flip and sort

Google Account
Your identity for all Google tools
Autosave
Changes are saved continuously
Shared with me
Files others gave you access to
Viewer
Can read only
Commenter
Can read, comment and suggest
Editor
Can change the file
keyPoints: Viewer reads, Commenter suggests, Editor changes.
Restricted means only the people you name.
Give the least access that works, and review it when a project ends.

practical.title: Practical: organise a Drive
practical.intro: Create a clean structure for something real.
steps: Create a folder for your current course or project with three folders inside it.
Make or upload three files and give each a good name with the date first.
Share the project folder with one friend as Commenter and check the sharing list.
Star the file you use most.

questions.text: Why does Workspace not have a Save button?
questions.explanation: Changes are saved continuously.

questions.text: How long does Drive keep deleted files in Trash?
questions.explanation: Trash keeps files for 30 days before removing them permanently.

questions.text: Which access suits a final newsletter for parents?
questions.explanation: Parents only need to read it.

questions.text: A friend needs to suggest edits but not change your text. Which role?
questions.explanation: Commenter allows comments and suggestions.

questions.explanation: A date, a subject and a version make it clear.

options: So they cannot keep seeing or changing your files
questions.explanation: Old access is a quiet risk.

questions.text: Why is 'Anyone with the link, Editor' risky?
options: Anyone with the link can change or delete the file
questions.explanation: The link may reach people you did not intend.

modules.title: Docs that work
modules.summary: Write structured documents with styles and lists, work with tables, and collaborate with comments, suggestions and version history.
modules.outcome: You can produce a clear document, work on it with others without chaos, and recover from mistakes.
modules.intro: A good document is easy to scan: a title, headings that tell the story, short paragraphs, lists where things come in sequence. Google Docs does the layout for you if you use its styles. This module teaches the habits of people whose documents get read.

topics.title: Styles and structure
topics.html:
In Docs you do not make a heading by making text big and bold. You apply a paragraph style from the box in the toolbar (Normal text, Title, Heading 1, Heading 2, Heading 3). A real heading tells Docs, and screen readers, and search, that this is a section title.

Why use real styles
With real heading stylesWith big bold text
The Outline panel lists every section so you can jump to itDocs does not know it is a heading
Change the look of all Heading 2s in one goChange each one by hand
Screen readers announce the structureA blind reader hears a wall of text
A table of contents builds itselfYou type one yourself
Worked example

Structure a short report

Water use at school: method, findings, recommendation.

  1. The first line is the Title.
  2. Method, Findings and Recommendation are Heading 2.
  3. Under Findings, the three results are a bulleted list.
  4. Open the Outline panel: the three sections should read as a clear plan.

Answer. If the Outline reads like a good plan, the document will read well.

Tip

Shortcuts: Ctrl+Alt+1 for Heading 1, Ctrl+Alt+2 for Heading 2, Ctrl+Alt+0 for Normal text. Ctrl+/ shows every shortcut.

Common mistakes

  • Pressing Enter twice for space instead of changing paragraph spacing.
  • Using spaces or the Tab key to line things up: use a table or a list.
  • Ten different fonts: pick one or two and stay with them.
  • A heading at the bottom of a page with its text on the next page.

Check what you just learned

1. How do you make a real heading in Docs?
  • Make text big and bold
  • Press Enter twice
  • Underline it
  • Apply a heading style (correct)

A heading style tells Docs it is a section title.

2. What does the Outline panel show?
  • The headings of your document (correct)
  • Spelling mistakes
  • Your contacts
  • The word count only

It lists the headings so you can jump around.
keyPoints: Use paragraph styles for titles and headings.
The Outline panel shows your structure.
Real structure helps readers, screen readers and search.

topics.title: Lists, tables and tidy layout
topics.html:
Use a list when items belong together, and a table when facts line up in rows and columns. Both are faster to read than a paragraph.

List or table?
You have...UseExample
Items in no particular orderBulleted listThings to bring
Steps in a sequenceNumbered listInstructions, action items
Things with several facts eachTableName, role, phone
Tasks to tick offChecklistA packing list
Worked example

Meeting minutes

You took rough notes in a meeting.

  1. Make the first line a Title and give each part a Heading 2.
  2. Turn the three names and their roles into a three-row, two-column table.
  3. Turn the actions into a numbered list and bold the deadline.

Answer. Minutes with a table and numbered actions are faster to act on than a page of text.

Table tips

  • Put the headings in the first row and make them bold.
  • Keep one fact per cell.
  • Avoid tables for layout: use them for data only.
  • Use Format > Table > Table properties to set borders and padding.
Tip

To add a row at the end of a table, click in the last cell and press Tab.

Watch out

Do not use a table to position pictures or to fake columns of text. Screen readers read tables cell by cell and become confusing.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is best for the steps of a recipe?
  • Bulleted list
  • Numbered list (correct)
  • Table
  • Heading 1

Steps happen in order, so number them.

2. When should you use a table?
  • To fake columns of text
  • For a title
  • For facts that line up in rows and columns (correct)
  • For colour

Tables are for data.
keyPoints: Lists for items; tables for facts in rows and columns.
Numbered lists show order; bulleted lists do not.
Header row first, one fact per cell.

topics.title: Comments, suggestions and version history
topics.html:
Docs has three tools that let people work on one file without stepping on each other.

Three collaboration tools
ToolWhat it doesUse when
CommentA note attached to a selection; can be replied to and resolvedYou have a question or a general note
Suggesting modeYour edits appear as suggestions the owner can accept or rejectYou edit someone else's work and want them to decide
Version historyEvery earlier version, with who changed whatYou need to go back, or see who made a change
Worked example

Recover from a mistake

Someone deleted a whole section last night.

  1. Open File > Version history > See version history.
  2. Pick last night's version from the list.
  3. Read it, then choose Restore this version, or copy only the lost section back.

Answer. Version history means no mistake in a shared document is permanent.

Etiquette for shared documents

  • Use comments and @mentions to ask a person a question; they get an email.
  • Switch to Suggesting when editing someone else's text.
  • Resolve a comment when it is dealt with; do not delete other people's comments.
  • Name a version (File > Version history > Name current version) before big changes.
Tip

Type @ followed by a name in a comment to notify that person and, if they cannot yet see the file, offer to share it.

Check what you just learned

1. You are editing a classmate's essay and want them to approve each change. Use:
  • Editing mode
  • Print preview
  • Viewing mode
  • Suggesting mode (correct)

Suggestions can be accepted or rejected one by one.

2. Where can you go back to last night's version?
  • Version history (correct)
  • Trash
  • Outline
  • Explore

Version history lists every earlier version.

Key terms: flip and sort

Paragraph style
Title, Heading 1, Normal text and so on
Outline
A panel listing the headings
Suggesting mode
Edits appear as suggestions to accept or reject
Comment
A note attached to text
Version history
Every earlier version of a file
@mention
Notifies a person inside a comment
keyPoints: Comments ask, suggestions propose, version history restores.
Use Suggesting mode on other people's text.
Name a version before a big change.

practical.title: Practical: a well-structured document
practical.intro: Write a one-page document on a topic you know.
steps: Write a title and three section headings using heading styles.
Add a bulleted list and a small table.
Share it with a friend as Commenter and ask them to leave two comments.
Reply to the comments, resolve them, and name the final version.

questions.text: Why use heading styles instead of big bold text?
options: Docs, screen readers and search understand the structure
questions.explanation: Real headings carry meaning as well as looks.

questions.text: Which tool shows your edits as proposals?
questions.explanation: Suggesting mode lets the owner accept or reject.

questions.text: What do you use to see who changed a sentence yesterday?
questions.explanation: Version history records who changed what.

questions.text: Which is the better choice for a sequence of steps?
questions.explanation: Numbers show order.

questions.text: Why avoid a table for layout?
options: Screen readers read it cell by cell and it becomes confusing
questions.explanation: Tables are for data.

questions.text: What does resolving a comment do?
options: Marks the note as dealt with
questions.explanation: Resolving closes the conversation and keeps it in history.

questions.text: Pressing Enter twice for extra space is a poor habit because:
options: It makes empty paragraphs; use paragraph spacing instead
questions.explanation: Empty paragraphs create messy spacing and structure.

modules.title: Sheets for teams
modules.summary: Use Sheets to calculate, flag, summarise and chart, and to keep clean data a team can trust.
modules.outcome: You can build a shared tracker or budget with formulas, drop-down choices, filters and a chart.
modules.intro: Sheets is Google's spreadsheet. If you have used a spreadsheet before, you already know the grid, the formula bar and the way formulas begin with an equals sign. What makes Sheets special is that a whole team can edit the same data at once, so it becomes the place for trackers, budgets and shared lists.

topics.title: Formulas and functions that you use every week
topics.html:
A formula begins with = and can use cell references (B2), operators (+ - * /) and functions (SUM, AVERAGE, IF, COUNTIF). Change a cell and every formula that depends on it updates.

Functions worth knowing first
FunctionDoesExample
SUMAdds numbers=SUM(D2:D4)
AVERAGEThe mean=AVERAGE(B2:B20)
IFChooses between two answers=IF(B2<15,"Remind","OK")
COUNTIFCounts matching cells=COUNTIF(C2:C6,"Remind")
SUMIFAdds matching rows=SUMIF(A2:A7,"Pen",B2:B7)
TODAYToday's date=TODAY()
Worked example

A class-trip budget

25 students; two buses at 6,000 each; tickets 150 each; lunch 120 each.

  1. Cost of each line: quantity times price, =B2*C2.
  2. Total: =SUM(D2:D4), which is 18,750.
  3. Each student pays: =D5/B6, which is 750.
  4. Change the price of a ticket and the total and the share update by themselves.

Answer. Never type a calculated number; let a formula calculate it.

Things that are only in Sheets

  • IMPORTRANGE pulls data from another spreadsheet, so one sheet can feed another.
  • QUERY filters and groups data with a few words, a bit like a small database question.
  • ARRAYFORMULA fills a whole column from one formula.
  • GOOGLEFINANCE and GOOGLETRANSLATE bring in live prices and translations.
Tip

Type = in a cell and start a function name: Sheets suggests it and shows a hint of the arguments. Press Tab to accept.

Watch out

Dates and numbers typed with the wrong format become text and will not calculate. If a SUM looks wrong, check that the numbers are right-aligned.

Check what you just learned

1. Which function counts how many cells say Remind?
  • SUM
  • COUNTIF (correct)
  • AVERAGE
  • TODAY

COUNTIF counts the cells that match a condition.

2. Why use a formula instead of typing a total?
  • It looks professional
  • Typing is forbidden
  • It updates when the numbers change (correct)
  • It prints faster

Formulas keep results correct as data changes.
keyPoints: Formulas start with = and update when cells change.
SUM, AVERAGE, IF, COUNTIF and SUMIF cover most weekly jobs.
Let formulas calculate; do not type results.

topics.title: Clean data: formats, drop-downs and validation
topics.html:
Shared sheets go wrong when people type things in different ways: Yes, yes, Y, yeah. A team tracker is only as good as its data, so make the right answer the easy answer.

Tools that keep data clean
ToolWhat it doesWhere
Drop-down (data validation)Lets people choose from a list instead of typingData > Data validation
Number and date formatsMake 0.256 show as 25.6% and a number show as a dateFormat > Number
Conditional formattingColours a cell by its value, for example red when overdueFormat > Conditional formatting
Freeze rowsKeeps the headings visible while you scrollView > Freeze
Protected rangesStops people editing formulas and headingsData > Protect sheets and ranges
Worked example

A task tracker

Five people update a task list.

  1. Status column: add a drop-down with Not started, In progress, Done.
  2. Conditional formatting: green when Done, amber when In progress.
  3. Freeze the heading row so it stays visible.
  4. Protect the formula column that counts tasks so nobody overwrites it.

Answer. People pick instead of type, so the counts are right every time.

Rules of a tidy shared sheet

  • One row per item, one fact per column.
  • A heading row, and no merged cells in the data.
  • No blank rows inside the table.
  • Inputs and formulas in separate columns, formulas protected.

Common mistakes

  • Merged cells in the middle of data, which break sorting and filtering.
  • Typing units into number cells (500 kg) so they become text.
  • Colour used as the only way to show status: also write the word.

Check what you just learned

1. What stops five people typing the same answer five different ways?
  • A bigger font
  • Autosave
  • A merged cell
  • A drop-down list (correct)

A drop-down makes the correct answer the easy answer.

2. Why avoid merged cells in the data?
  • They break sorting and filtering (correct)
  • They are ugly
  • They cost money
  • They hide formulas

Data tools expect one value per cell.
keyPoints: Drop-downs and validation keep data consistent.
Conditional formatting shows status at a glance.
Freeze headings, protect formulas, avoid merged cells.

topics.title: Sorting, filtering and charting
topics.html:
Once the data is clean, three moves turn it into answers: sort it, filter it, chart it.

Sort, filter or filter view?
MoveEffectWho sees it
Sort rangeRearranges rows, for everyoneEveryone (it changes the data order)
FilterHides rows that do not matchEveryone who opens the sheet (it is saved with the sheet)
Filter viewYour own filter and sort, saved by nameOnly you, until you share it
Worked example

A chart that answers a question

Which members attended fewest sessions?

  1. Select the names and the sessions columns.
  2. Insert > Chart and choose a Column chart.
  3. Sort the data from lowest to highest first so the shortest bars sit on one side.
  4. Give the chart a title that states the point: Four members are below 15 sessions.

Answer. A chart should answer a question, not decorate a sheet.

Watch out

Always sort the whole table, not a single column. If you sort one column alone the other columns stay where they were and every row is now wrong.

Tip

Use a filter view when you only want to look at your own tasks; a normal filter would change what everybody else sees.

Check what you just learned

1. Which tool lets you filter without changing what others see?
  • Sort range
  • Filter view (correct)
  • Merge cells
  • Freeze

A filter view is your own saved view.

2. Why sort the whole table rather than one column?
  • It is faster
  • Excel forbids it
  • Rows would no longer match across columns (correct)
  • It saves memory

The other columns would stay put and the rows would be wrong.

Key terms: flip and sort

Formula
A calculation starting with =
Data validation
Rules or drop-downs that limit what can be typed
Conditional formatting
Colour that changes with the value
Filter view
A private saved filter and sort
IMPORTRANGE
Pulls data from another spreadsheet
Protected range
Cells others cannot edit
keyPoints: Sort the whole table; filter to focus; chart to answer a question.
A filter view is private to you.
Give charts a title that states the finding.

practical.title: Practical: a team tracker
practical.intro: Build a tracker you could really share.
steps: Make a table of at least eight tasks with owner, due date and status.
Add a drop-down for status and colour the cells with conditional formatting.
Add a COUNTIF that counts the tasks not yet done.
Freeze the heading row and protect the formula cell.

questions.text: What does every formula begin with?
questions.explanation: A formula starts with =.

questions.text: Which function adds only the rows that match a condition?
questions.explanation: SUMIF adds matching rows.

questions.text: Which Sheets function pulls data from another spreadsheet?
questions.explanation: IMPORTRANGE links sheets together.

questions.text: A drop-down list in a cell is made with:
questions.explanation: Data validation limits what can be entered.

questions.text: Why not use colour alone for status?
options: Some people cannot see the difference, so also write the word
questions.explanation: Accessible sheets do not rely on colour alone.

questions.text: Which is private to you?
questions.explanation: A filter view is saved for you.

questions.text: A SUM gives a surprisingly low answer. One likely cause is:
questions.explanation: Text numbers are skipped by SUM.

modules.title: Slides that present
modules.summary: Plan a talk, build clear slides with themes, layouts and diagrams, and present with notes and confidence.
modules.outcome: You can make a short deck that supports your voice instead of competing with it, and present it from Slides.
modules.intro: Slides support a talk; they are not the talk. The best decks have few words, one idea per slide and a design that stays out of the way. Google Slides gives you themes, layouts and shapes; your job is to use them lightly.

topics.title: Plan the talk before you open Slides
topics.html:
The most common mistake is opening Slides and typing. A talk starts as a message, a handful of points and a sense of who is listening.

A simple five-slide structure for a short pitch
SlideJobExample
1. TitleName the topicRecycle Right
2. The problemWhy should anyone care?One bin for everything
3. Our ideaWhat you proposeThree labelled bins
4. What we needThe askTwo bins, posters, ten minutes
5. Thank youClose and invite questionsQuestions?
Worked example

From message to slides

Your message: Three labelled bins will cut our waste.

  1. Point 1: today every item goes in one bin.
  2. Point 2: three bins separate paper, plastic and food.
  3. Point 3: students and posters make it easy.
  4. Each point becomes a slide whose title is the point, with two or three short bullets.

Answer. A slide title that says the point (not just a topic) is the single best habit.

Tip

Write the slide titles in a Doc first. If the titles read like a story, the deck will too.

Watch out

If your slide has a paragraph on it, your audience will read it and stop listening to you. Put the detail in the speaker notes.

Check what you just learned

1. What should you decide first?
  • The theme colour
  • The animation
  • The font size
  • Who is listening and your one-sentence message (correct)

Everything else depends on the message and the audience.

2. Where does the detail go?
  • In the speaker notes (correct)
  • On the slide in small text
  • In the footer
  • Nowhere

Notes hold what you say; the slide holds the point.
keyPoints: Plan the message and three points before building.
A slide title that states the point beats a topic label.
Detail goes in speaker notes, not on the slide.

topics.title: Themes, layouts and readable slides
topics.html:
A theme sets the fonts, colours and background for every slide. A layout sets where things go on one slide (title, title and body, two columns, section header). Use them and your deck looks consistent with almost no effort.

Choosing a layout
You want...Layout
To open the talkTitle slide
A point with a few bulletsTitle and body
A before-and-after or two listsTwo columns
To mark a new partSection header
A picture to speak for itselfTitle only or blank, with the picture

Rules for readable slides

  • Few words. Aim for no more than about five short bullets, and each bullet a few words.
  • Large text. Nothing smaller than about 24 points; if it will not fit, split the slide.
  • High contrast. Dark text on a light background, or the reverse, never grey on grey.
  • One idea per slide.
  • Consistent. Change the theme once in the master, not slide by slide.

Common mistakes

  • Reading the slide aloud word for word.
  • A different font and size on every slide.
  • Text over a busy picture so it cannot be read.
  • More than three colours.
Tip

Open Slide > Edit theme (the master) to change the font or colour for the whole deck at once.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use layouts?
  • To add animation
  • To keep titles and text in consistent places (correct)
  • To save storage
  • To print faster

Layouts put the same things in the same place on each slide.

2. How many ideas should one slide hold?
  • As many as fit
  • Ten
  • One (correct)
  • Three paragraphs

One idea per slide is easier to follow.
keyPoints: Themes give consistency; layouts give each slide a structure.
Few words, large text, high contrast, one idea.
Change the master, not every slide.

topics.title: Diagrams, notes and presenting
topics.html:
A diagram shows a process faster than bullets. Use shapes and arrows (Insert > Shape) and keep their text tiny: a box that says Sort beats a paragraph.

Worked example

A process in four boxes

How a bottle is reborn: collected, sorted, melted, made new.

  1. Draw four rounded boxes in a row.
  2. Type one word in each: Collect, Sort, Melt, Make.
  3. Join them with arrows.
  4. Give the slide a title that states the point: One bottle can become a new one.

Answer. A reader gets the whole process in two seconds.

Presenting well

  • Open Present (or Ctrl+F5) and rehearse aloud at least once.
  • Use speaker notes (View > Show speaker notes) to hold your detail; the audience does not see them.
  • Face the audience, not the screen.
  • Use the Q&A feature in Present mode to take questions from the audience on their phones.
  • Have the file open offline or exported to PDF in case the internet fails.
Useful presenting keys
KeyDoes
Right arrow or SpaceNext slide
Left arrowPrevious slide
BBlack screen (to focus attention on you)
EscLeave presenting
Watch out

Never rely on the venue's internet. Download a PDF or make the deck available offline before you present.

Try it yourself: You have ten minutes. About how many slides?

Model answer. Around eight to ten. A common guide is about one to two minutes per slide, with fewer slides if each has an idea that takes time to explain.

Check what you just learned

1. Where does detail you will say aloud belong?
  • On the slide
  • In the title
  • In the theme
  • In speaker notes (correct)

Notes are visible only to you.

2. What is a sensible backup if the internet fails?
  • An exported PDF or an offline copy (correct)
  • Hope
  • A bigger screen
  • Fewer slides

A local copy works without the internet.

Key terms: flip and sort

Theme
Fonts, colours and background for the whole deck
Layout
Where things sit on one slide
Master
The template all slides inherit from
Speaker notes
Your private notes under each slide
Present mode
Full-screen slideshow
Q&A
A way for the audience to ask questions during the talk
keyPoints: Shapes and arrows show a process quickly.
Speaker notes hold detail the audience does not need to read.
Rehearse aloud and keep an offline copy.

modules.title: Forms and surveys
modules.summary: Design a form that people will finish, choose the right question types, and turn the answers into something useful.
modules.outcome: You can plan, build and read a survey or quiz, and avoid the mistakes that spoil results.
modules.intro: Forms collects answers from many people and puts every response in a Sheet automatically. It is the right tool for sign-ups, feedback, quizzes and registrations. A good form is short, clear and aimed at one decision.

topics.title: Ask the right question the right way
topics.html:
The question type decides how easy it is to answer and how easy it is to analyse. Choose the type that limits the answer to what you can use.

Question types
TypeUse forExample
Multiple choiceOne answer from a short listWhich lunch slot do you prefer?
CheckboxesSeveral answers from a listWhich clubs would you join?
Drop-downOne answer from a long listWhich class are you in?
Linear scaleA rating you can averageRate the workshop from 1 to 5
Short answerA word or numberYour admission number
ParagraphAn open opinionWhat would you change?
Date or timeA clean dateWhen would you like the meeting?
Worked example

Good and poor wording

You want feedback on a workshop.

  1. Poor: Was the workshop good and useful? Two questions in one; nobody knows which to answer.
  2. Better: How useful was the workshop? (1 not at all to 5 very).
  3. Poor: Don't you agree the workshop was excellent? A leading question.
  4. Better: What would you change about the workshop?

Answer. Ask one thing at a time, in neutral words.

Rules for good questions

  • One question, one idea.
  • Neutral wording: do not push people towards an answer.
  • A fixed list wherever you can, so answers can be counted.
  • Mark essential questions Required, and nothing else.
  • Keep it short. Every extra question loses some people.

Common mistakes

  • Asking for information you will not use.
  • Two questions in one.
  • Scales without labels at each end.
  • Making every question Required.

Check what you just learned

1. Which type suits 'Which of these would you join? (pick any)'?
  • Multiple choice
  • Checkboxes (correct)
  • Date
  • Paragraph

People may choose several, so use checkboxes.

2. Which wording is better?
  • Don't you agree the workshop was excellent?
  • Was it good and useful and fun?
  • How useful was the workshop, from 1 to 5? (correct)
  • Tell us everything

A neutral, single, answerable question.
keyPoints: Choose the type that limits the answer to what you can count.
One question, one idea, neutral wording.
Only mark essential questions Required.

topics.title: Build, share and protect a form
topics.html:
A form is built from questions grouped into sections. Settings decide who can fill it and how.

Important settings
SettingWhat it doesUse it when
RequiredThe question must be answeredYou really need the answer
Response validationChecks the answer fits a rule (a number, an email, a length)You want clean data
SectionsSplits a long form into pagesA form has more than about ten questions
Limit to 1 responseEach person can answer once (they must sign in)A vote or a registration
Quiz modeGives a score and feedbackA test, not a survey
Collect email addressesRecords who answeredYou need to follow up, and have told them

Before you send

  • Fill it in yourself on a phone.
  • Ask one other person to try it.
  • Check the thank-you message and the closing date.
  • Do not ask for passwords or sensitive information.
Watch out

Never ask for passwords, card numbers or other sensitive details in a form. A form is not a secure place for secrets, and people should not be trained to type them into links.

Tip

Responses land in a linked Sheet (Responses > Link to Sheets). Use it for charts and for formulas such as COUNTIF.

Check what you just learned

1. Which setting stops a vote from being answered twice by the same person?
  • Required
  • Paragraph
  • Sections
  • Limit to 1 response (correct)

It allows one response per signed-in person.

2. Where should you check the form before sharing?
  • Fill it in yourself, ideally on a phone too (correct)
  • Only on your laptop
  • Nowhere
  • In Drive

Test it as a respondent would.
keyPoints: Draft first, build, preview, then share.
Validation and Required keep the data clean.
Never ask for passwords or card details.

topics.title: Read the results
topics.html:
Forms shows a summary of each question as a chart, and keeps every response as a row in a Sheet. Use both.

Where to look
ViewGood for
SummaryA quick picture: pie charts for choices, bars for scales, a list for open answers
QuestionThe answers to one question at a time
IndividualOne person's whole response
Linked SheetSorting, filtering, formulas and your own charts
Worked example

Turn feedback into a decision

Forty people rated a workshop 1 to 5 and wrote one open comment.

  1. In the linked Sheet find the average rating with =AVERAGE(B2:B41).
  2. Count how many gave 4 or 5: =COUNTIF(B2:B41,">=4").
  3. Read the open comments and group them under two or three themes.
  4. Write one sentence of insight and one action.

Answer. A survey is only useful when it ends in a decision.

Watch out

A small, self-selected sample can mislead. If only the keenest people answered, the results may be more positive than the whole group feels. Say how many people answered.

A short report from a survey

  1. How many people answered, out of how many asked.
  2. The two or three most important findings, with numbers.
  3. A chart for the one finding that matters most.
  4. What you will do about it.

Check what you just learned

1. Where do you do your own calculations on responses?
  • In the form editor
  • In the linked Sheet (correct)
  • In Slides
  • In Gmail

Responses are saved as rows in a Sheet.

2. Why say how many people answered?
  • To look big
  • Because Forms requires it
  • A small or self-selected group may not represent everyone (correct)
  • To save space

Readers need to judge how far to trust the result.

Key terms: flip and sort

Form
A set of questions that collects responses
Required
A question that must be answered
Response validation
A rule an answer must meet
Linked Sheet
The Sheet that stores responses
Quiz mode
A form with scoring and feedback
Sample
The people who answered
keyPoints: Use the Summary for a quick picture and the linked Sheet for analysis.
Say how many people answered.
End with a decision.

modules.title: Collaborate and stay safe
modules.summary: Work together smoothly with Calendar and Meet, keep your account and files safe, and run a small project across Drive, Docs, Sheets and Slides.
modules.outcome: You can coordinate a team project in Workspace and protect your account from the most common problems.
modules.intro: Tools are only half of working together. The other half is habits: where decisions are recorded, who can see what, and how to avoid the mistakes that cost teams a day. This module ties the tools into a way of working, and teaches the few safety habits that matter most.

topics.title: A way of working for a team
topics.html:
Teams that work well in Workspace follow a small number of rules. They are simple, and they save a lot of confusion.

A simple team setup
NeedToolHabit
One place for all filesA shared folder in DriveEverything for the project lives there, with a clear folder tree
The planA DocGoals, owners and dates in one document with headings and a task table
Who does what by whenA SheetA tracker with owner, due date and status drop-downs
Talking things throughMeet and chatShort calls with an agenda and notes written afterwards
Dates everyone seesCalendarAdd milestones and invite the team so they appear on everyone's calendar
Showing progressSlidesOne short deck for each update
Worked example

Run a school event

Five students organise a cleanliness week.

  1. Make a shared folder, Cleanliness Week, and share it with the five students as Editors and the teacher as Commenter.
  2. Write the plan in one Doc: goals, a task table with owners and dates, and next steps.
  3. Track progress in a Sheet with a Status drop-down.
  4. Put each milestone on a shared Calendar and use Meet for a ten-minute check-in each Monday.

Answer. One folder, one plan, one tracker: nobody asks which version is the latest.

Habits that keep a team out of trouble

  • One source of truth. Link to the file; do not email attachments.
  • Name an owner for every task and every file.
  • Write decisions down in the Doc, not only in chat.
  • Meet with an agenda, and end with who does what by when.
Tip

Paste a Drive link into an email or chat instead of attaching the file. Everyone then opens the same, latest copy.

Check what you just learned

1. Why share a link instead of emailing an attachment?
  • Links are shorter
  • Links are faster
  • Attachments are illegal
  • Everyone sees the same latest version (correct)

A link points at one living file.

2. What belongs in the task tracker?
  • Owner, due date and status for each task (correct)
  • Only ideas
  • Pictures
  • Passwords

A tracker shows who does what by when.
keyPoints: One shared folder, one plan, one tracker.
Link to files; do not email copies.
Name an owner, and write decisions down.

topics.title: Calendar and Meet
topics.html:
Calendar shows when things happen; Meet is where a call happens. Together they replace most of the 'when are we meeting?' messages.

Good calendar habits
DoBecause
Give every event a clear title and a description with the agendaPeople know why they are invited
Add a Meet link to the eventEveryone joins with one click
Check availability before you inviteAvoids clashes
Add remindersFewer missed meetings
Attach the notes Doc to the eventThe meeting and its notes stay together

Running a good meeting

  1. Share the agenda in the event description.
  2. Start on time and name a note-taker.
  3. Use Present to share the screen when you review a Slides deck or a Sheet.
  4. End by reading the actions aloud: who, what, by when.
  5. Send the notes the same day.
Watch out

Be careful about recording or sharing a call: ask everyone first, and check the rules of your school or organisation.

Try it yourself: A meeting runs over. What is the most useful thing to do in the last minute?

Model answer. Read out the actions: who does what by when. Then the next steps are clear even if the discussion was long.

Check what you just learned

1. What should an event description contain?
  • Nothing
  • The agenda (correct)
  • A joke
  • A password

An agenda tells people what the meeting is for.

2. How do you end a meeting well?
  • Say goodbye
  • Delete the notes
  • Read the actions: who, what, by when (correct)
  • Start another meeting

Clear actions are the point of a meeting.
keyPoints: A clear title, an agenda and a Meet link make a good event.
Attach the notes Doc to the event.
End meetings by reading out the actions.

topics.title: Keep your account and files safe
topics.html:
Your Google Account is the key to your email, your files and often your other accounts. A few habits protect nearly all of it.

Safe and risky habits
HabitSafe or riskyWhy
Turn on 2-Step VerificationSafeA second proof stops someone who only has your password
One strong password per account (a password manager helps)SafeA leak at one site cannot open the others
One password everywhereRiskyOne leak opens everything
Sign in only from the real Google address, typed or bookmarkedSafeAvoids fake pages
Typing your password into a page from an unexpected emailRiskyIt may be a fake sign-in page
Review sharing and remove people when a project endsSafeOld access is a quiet risk
Anyone with the link as EditorRiskyAnyone with the link can change or delete the file

Spot a phishing message

  • It creates urgency: Your account will close in one hour.
  • It asks you to sign in or confirm details through a link.
  • The sender or link looks slightly wrong.
  • It asks for something unusual, such as gift cards or a password.
  • If in doubt, do not click: go to the site yourself, or ask a trusted person.
Worked example

Check your account

Ten minutes, once in a while.

  1. Open your Google Account's security page.
  2. Check that 2-Step Verification is on.
  3. Look at the devices signed in and remove any you do not know.
  4. Look at which apps have access and remove those you no longer use.

Answer. Small, regular checks stop most account problems.

Watch out

No real organisation will ask you for your password by email or message. If a message asks, it is a scam.

Check what you just learned

1. What does 2-Step Verification add?
  • A longer password
  • A faster login
  • More storage
  • A second proof that it is really you (correct)

It protects you if your password is stolen.

2. An email says your account will close in an hour unless you sign in through its link. What do you do?
  • Do not click; go to the site yourself or ask someone (correct)
  • Click quickly
  • Reply with your password
  • Forward it to everyone

Urgency and a sign-in link are classic signs of phishing.

Key terms: flip and sort

Shared folder
One folder the whole team uses
Single source of truth
One file everyone uses
2-Step Verification
A second proof when signing in
Phishing
A fake message that tries to steal details
Agenda
What a meeting will cover
Owner
The person responsible for a task or file
keyPoints: Turn on 2-Step Verification and use a unique password.
Do not click sign-in links in unexpected messages.
Review sharing and devices from time to time.
